lesson_title: Boxes, Balloons and Jugs: the Mole at Grade 11
hook_text: Nobody counts 500 sweets at the till. They count boxes. Chemists count boxes of 602 000 000 000 000 000 000 000.
clip_script: Nobody at a tuck shop counts out five hundred loose sweets. They count boxes, because every box holds the same number. Chemistry has exactly one box size for everything in the universe: 6,02 times 10 to the 23 particles. That box is called a mole. Here's the trick — a box of marshmallows and a box of toothpicks hold the same COUNT but different WEIGHTS. Same in chemistry: a mole of hydrogen weighs 1 gram, a mole of carbon dioxide weighs 44. The periodic table is just the catalogue of box weights. Grams to boxes? Divide by the box weight. Gases are even better: at standard conditions every gas, light or heavy, packs one box into 22,4 cubic decimetres — two shopping bags of space — because a gas is mostly emptiness and only the count matters. And solutions? Concentration is boxes per jug. One scoop in a small jug is strong; the same scoop in a bucket is weak. Boxes, balloons, jugs. That's the entire chapter.
visual_style: A tuck-shop counter with identical boxes on a scale showing different masses; cut to two equal balloons with wildly different scale readings; end on two jugs, one small and vivid, one large and pale.
mood: Playful and demystifying — the scariest number in chemistry turned into shopping.
pacing: Quick counter open, three clean beats for boxes, balloons and jugs, snap ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make every mole question a two-step conversion.
